CHAPTER 1: ECONOMICS AS A WAY OF THINKING

WHY STUDY ECONOMICS?
- Economics helps you understand economic matters you meet as a consumer and as a citizen.
- It broadens your understanding of the economic, social and environmental issues facing Ireland and the world.
- Economics affects daily life: funding for your school, the quality of food in the school canteen, the quality of your nearest hospital, the prices you pay for goods and services, and the choices you make with the resources you have (e.g. choosing to study economics).
- Financial institutions: you may have an account with a bank, the post office or a credit union. Some financial institutions may not always have your best interests at heart, which is why they need to be regulated (Chapter 15).
- National debt: previous generations are passing a national debt on to you. Some of the tax you pay across your working life will go towards paying the interest/capital of that debt (Chapter 12).
- Good decisions by previous generations: opening the economy to international trade in the late 1950s (Chapter 18) and reducing corporation tax (tax on trading profits) to 12.5% in the 1990s helped make Ireland the second most developed nation in the world, as measured by the Human Development Index (HDI) (Chapter 16).
- Economic history: you will learn about the Great Depression, the Celtic Tiger years, the Financial Crash, Brexit and the Covid-19 pandemic.
- Most importantly, economics helps you make better, more informed choices about contributing to a sustainable world that takes account of the needs of those around us and of future generations.

ASSESSMENT
- Final exam: 80% of marks. 2 hours 30 minutes for both Ordinary and Higher Level.
- Research study: 20% of marks. A common research study brief is issued to Ordinary and Higher Level students at the start of Sixth Year.

POSITIVE AND NORMATIVE ECONOMIC STATEMENTS
- Positive economic statement: a precise, fact-based statement based on data, facts and figures. It can be proved (tested) with data.
- Normative economic statement: a statement about how things SHOULD be. It is like an opinion, based on the value judgements of the person making it, and is not backed up with data to prove it is correct.
- Tip: normative statements often contain the word "should".
- Examples of positive statements (Table 1.1):
- A rise in unemployment results in a fall in incomes.
- The sugar-sweetened drinks tax has resulted in a fall in demand for sugary drinks.
- As carbon taxes on fossil fuels continue to rise, sales of electric vehicles (EVs) have risen.
- The rise in excise duty on tobacco has reduced demand for cigarettes while increasing the popularity of vaping.
- When demand for Irish exports rises, so too does employment in exporting firms.
- Price increases are the most effective way to discourage smoking, particularly among young people.
- Examples of normative statements (Table 1.1):
- The government should increase child benefit in order to reduce poverty levels.
- The government should abolish USC (Universal Social Charge) to increase demand in the economy.
- The government should supply basic health care to all citizens.
- The price of milk should be 3 euro per litre to ensure farming families have decent incomes.
- The government should raise the minimum wage to reduce poverty.
- Why it matters: economists, governments, the media and the public use both kinds of statement. The research study requires you to back up your research with data, so you will use positive statements in particular.

DIFFERENT SOLUTIONS TO ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
- Normative statements can make solutions seem obvious, but there are many perspectives on how a problem might be solved.
- Example: homelessness. Obvious solution: the government builds more homes. Assume 1 billion euro would fund 10,000 new homes.
- The economic problem: the government has limited resources and must make choices.
- Opportunity cost: when a choice is made due to limited resources, the opportunity cost is the best alternative that is foregone.
- Example: the government has only 1 billion euro for capital spending and four projects, each costing 1 billion euro: Metrolink (a rail line in Dublin), the Limerick-Cork motorway, the Galway bypass, and 10,000 new homes for the homeless.
- If it chooses Metrolink, it foregoes the other three projects.
- Option: borrow to do all four. Problem: general government debt was forecast to reach almost 240 billion euro by 2021. Borrowed money must be repaid with interest by future taxpayers. The government already pays billions in interest each year.
- Option: raise corporation tax (tax on company profits) from 12.5% (one of the lowest in the world) to 15% or 20%. Problem: the 1,500 multinational corporations (MNCs) in Ireland might relocate some/all operations, and future MNC investment might be cut or cancelled, which could reduce government revenue in the future.
- Lesson: governments, firms and individuals face economic problems with many possible solutions.

SIGNIFICANT ECONOMIC EVENTS AND PERIODS

1. THE GREAT DEPRESSION (1929-1938)
- The most significant economic downturn of the 1900s in the Western World.
- The US economy expanded a lot in the 1920s. Millions of high and low income investors put savings and borrowed money into the New York Stock Market.
- Widespread speculation meant stock prices were much higher than their actual values.
- 24 October 1929 (Black Thursday): stock prices began to collapse as nervous investors sold. The Wall Street Crash caused huge losses.
- Investment spending (e.g. building/expanding a factory) fell, which increased unemployment.
- Rising unemployment and lower wages meant consumer spending fell a lot, leading to a downturn lasting a decade.
- Industrial production fell by over a half.
- Bank runs were common in the early 1930s, leading to bank failures and loss of savings.
- Bank run: when nervous depositors suddenly try to withdraw their deposits from a bank at the same time.
- Outcome for economic thinking: the importance of government injecting money into the economy to create jobs, increase consumer spending and grow the economy.
- John Maynard Keynes: economist who advocated using government spending to grow the economy.
- US President Franklin D. Roosevelt's 'New Deal' funded public works (bridges, dams, highways), creating jobs and stimulating demand.

2. THE 1950s AND 1960s IN IRELAND
- Since the foundation of the State, policy centred on self-sufficiency and trade protection (discouraging imports so Irish industry would grow).
- This policy was unsuccessful and left Ireland with: high unemployment; high emigration (over 400,000 emigrated in the 1950s); falling population (just below 2.9 million in 1956); low incomes and high taxes; overdependence on agriculture; low industrial development.
- 1958: public servants in the Department of Finance, led by T.K. Whitaker, produced a programme for economic expansion based on Whitaker's report 'Economic Development'.
- Focus: open the economy to international trade and move away from overdependence on a declining agricultural sector.
- By exporting, Irish firms would find new markets, expand and employ more people. Opening up would also increase Foreign Direct Investment (FDI).
- Result: economic growth and prosperity in the 1960s; employment rose and emigration fell.
- Exporting remains central to Irish economic policy (Chapter 18).

3. 1973: IRELAND JOINS THE EEC (NOW THE EU)
- After Brexit there are 27 EU member states, 19 of which are in the eurozone.
- Single market: the EU as one territory without internal borders or other obstacles to the free movement of goods, services, capital and people. It has contributed to growth and made life easier for businesses and consumers.
- Customs union: free trade between member states (no trade barriers such as tariffs) and a common external tariff for non-members.
- Trading bloc: a group of countries that have trade agreements with each other and put trade barriers (e.g. tariffs) on non-members, e.g. the EU.
- ADVANTAGES of EU membership for Ireland (Table 1.2):
- 1. Free movement of goods/services: Irish firms can sell without barriers to a potential market of 448 million people.
- 2. FDI: foreign firms locate in Ireland to get free access to the EU market. E.g. a Japanese firm in Ireland avoids tariffs it would face selling into the EU from Japan.
- 3. Higher employment due to free access to the EU market for exporters and due to FDI.
- 4. Free movement of people: Irish passport-holders can visit, live, work and study in other EU states, and vice versa.
- 5. The EU is a large, powerful trading bloc that negotiates trade deals for all members, putting Ireland in a stronger position than negotiating alone.
- DISADVANTAGES of EU membership for Ireland:
- 1. Firms in the other 26 member states can sell freely in Ireland. Good for consumers but Irish firms may lose business; spending on imports reduces Ireland's national income.
- 2. Contribution to the EU budget rises as GDP rises. Ireland's contribution in 2021 was expected to be 3.67 billion euro.
- 3. A member state cannot pass laws that contradict EU law - a loss of control. The Irish Government can be fined for not implementing EU law.
- 4. Fiscal rules: the Current Budget Deficit (CBD) cannot exceed 3% of GDP; public debt cannot exceed 60% of GDP.
- 5. A member state cannot make its own trade deals with non-EU countries.

THE SINGLE CURRENCY
- Ireland joined the euro in 1999; notes and coins arrived in 2002 (Chapter 14).

4. MID-1990s TO 2007: THE CELTIC TIGER
- Celtic Tiger: the period of significant year-on-year economic growth from the mid-1990s until 2007, also called 'the boom'.
- Increased FDI in the late 1990s led to more jobs, higher incomes and much higher exports.
- Consumer spending rose. Demand for property grew as emigration fell and many people immigrated for jobs.
- Property boom: strong demand led to continuous rises in property prices, fuelled by low-interest mortgages.
- Poor regulation of banks: some banks gave excessive loans to people with insecure jobs and lent recklessly to property developers.
- The cost of doing business rose and Ireland lost some attractiveness for foreign investment; some MNCs relocated. This was masked by jobs and growth in construction.
- Government current income rose (e.g. stamp duty on property transactions, indirect taxes on consumer spending). Current spending also rose (e.g. public sector pay and social welfare).

5. THE FINANCIAL CRISIS AND GREAT RECESSION (2008-2012)
- Lehman Brothers (a US bank) collapsed in 2008, affecting financial institutions worldwide, including Ireland.
- Sub-prime mortgages: US banks had given mortgages to 'sub-prime' borrowers (borrowers with poor credit ratings) and sold these debts to banks/investors around the world.
- When US interest rates rose, many sub-prime borrowers defaulted, causing huge problems for US institutions and those who had invested in them.
- Nervous banks became reluctant to lend to each other, causing a sudden pause in credit.
- In Ireland, property prices fell, many builders went bankrupt and could not repay loans; banks faced massive bad debts (unpaid loans); some depositors withdrew money.

THE BANK GUARANTEE (CREDIT INSTITUTIONS (FINANCIAL SUPPORT) SCHEME) - 30 SEPTEMBER 2008
- The state guaranteed the liabilities of certain banks: if a covered bank could not repay depositors, the government would provide the funds.
- Banks covered: AIB, EBS, Bank of Ireland, Irish Life & Permanent, Irish Nationwide Building Society and Anglo Irish Bank.
- Introduced because Anglo Irish Bank was about to run out of cash/capital (about to collapse). Its depositors could have lost their money, causing panic and bank runs on other banks.
- Bank run (fuller definition): depositors panic and lose confidence in their bank or the financial system and try to withdraw savings; since banks use deposits to fund lending, they can quickly run out of cash.
- Value of liabilities guaranteed: over 440 billion euro (worst case if all banks failed).
- Actual cost to the state (taxpayer): around 64 billion euro, much of it borrowed. Some recovered (e.g. sale of AIB shares) but much is in the national debt, to be repaid with interest by current and future taxpayers.
- Circumstances leading to the guarantee: banks borrowed from other banks (e.g. European banks) and bondholders during the boom and lent it to property developers and homebuyers; when property demand fell, developers could not repay; homeowners struggled due to rising unemployment; banks faced huge bad debts; bank share prices fell; depositors withdrew savings; banks struggled to raise cash (sell bonds) as investors would not lend.

THE BAILOUT (JANUARY 2011)
- Ireland entered a bailout programme worth 85 billion euro, of which 67.5 billion euro was borrowed.
- Troika: the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the European Commission and the European Central Bank (ECB).
- Make-up of the 85 billion euro: 22.5 billion from the IMF; 45 billion in loans from other EU countries; 12.5 billion from the National Pensions Reserve Fund; 5 billion cash reserves from the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA). (22.5 + 45 = 67.5 borrowed.)
- Why Ireland sought help: current revenue fell sharply (tax revenue fell in the recession); current spending rose (e.g. higher social welfare due to unemployment); the government struggled to borrow because Ireland was seen as high-risk; by late 2010 banks faced a liquidity crisis as depositors withdrew savings despite the guarantee.
- Role of the IMF: supports countries in economic crisis with loans (charging interest) when they cannot borrow normally. It releases funds in stages, as long as the government follows its instructions - usually raising taxes and cutting spending.
- Current budget deficit: when government current revenue is lower than government current spending, so the government must borrow the difference.
- Uses of the bailout: about 50 billion euro to fund current budget deficits in 2011, 2012 and 2013; the other 35 billion mainly to recapitalise/support banks.
- Implications of the bailout:
- Lower standard of living: spending cuts (social welfare, public sector pay bill) and higher revenue (Universal Social Charge, USC, introduced in 2011).
- Loss of sovereignty: the IMF and European Commission controlled Irish fiscal policy (spending and taxation) until December 2013.
- Interest charged on borrowed money.
- Banking restructured: two main 'pillar' banks, Bank of Ireland and AIB. Anglo Irish Bank and Irish Nationwide were liquidated.

6. ECONOMIC RECOVERY (2012-2019)
- Increased lending by financial institutions.
- Growth of the tourism industry.
- Increased FDI - corporation tax revenue rose significantly.
- Increased demand for Irish exports, e.g. medical drugs and devices, agri-food (beef, butter, cheese).
- Slightly lower taxes on labour near the end of the period raised disposable incomes and consumer spending.
- Recovery in construction due to demand for homes, offices, hotels and student accommodation.

7. BREXIT: UK VOTES TO LEAVE THE EU (23 JUNE 2016)
- Reasons for the referendum/leave vote:
- Free movement of people: an EU state cannot restrict immigration from other EU states. 2.37 million EU citizens worked in the UK in 2019 (Office of National Statistics). Leaving would let the UK control its borders and immigration.
- EU laws/regulations (e.g. environmental laws, product safety rules): leaving regained independence/sovereignty.
- Financial contribution: the claim the UK paid 350 million pounds per week to the EU budget. This ignored money received back (rebates, grants, farm subsidies) and the benefit of free access to over 448 million customers.
- The 'Brexit Bus' NHS pledge influenced many, especially elderly voters, but soon after the vote it was clear the savings would not go to the NHS.
- Ireland's ties with the UK: an important trading partner, a land bridge to mainland Europe, many British people live in Ireland and vice versa.
- Concerns, problems and opportunities for Ireland:
- 1. Free movement of goods/services at risk: without the December 2020 trade deal, trade would have faced tariffs and quotas. 2016-2020 was a time of huge uncertainty; businesses and government paid for contingency plans for a no-deal Brexit. Even with the deal, extra paperwork means extra costs and possible delays at ports.
- 2. Relocation of firms: Irish firms exporting to the UK had an incentive to move some operations to the UK; UK firms supplying the EU had an incentive to move to Ireland, the only remaining English-speaking EU country (e.g. Barclays Bank from the City of London).
- 3. Exchange rate: sterling fell sharply on the morning of the result, significantly raising the price of Irish exports to the UK (Chapter 18).

8. THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC
- Economic shock: an unpredictable event that affects an economy.
- Covid-19 was both a health emergency and an economic shock. Ireland, as an open economy dependent on international trade, was badly hit.
- Hospitality (hotels, restaurants, pubs, shops) hit by the halt to international tourism.
- Aviation suffered a sudden drop in demand.
- Entertainment hit by cancelled/postponed events and festivals.
- Government current revenue fell substantially.
- Government current spending rose: social welfare (Pandemic Unemployment Payment, PUP, initially 350 euro per week); health costs (testing and tracing, PPE, extra hospital staff).
- Extra financial supports for businesses.
- Investment decisions deferred or cancelled due to uncertainty.

LEARNING FROM HISTORY
- After the Celtic Tiger property crash, the Central Bank placed restrictions on the size of mortgages (Chapter 4).
- Poor regulation and reckless behaviour before 2008 led to much improved regulation and supervision of banks - a lesson costing the taxpayer 64 billion euro.
- The 12.5% corporation tax rate has helped attract over 1,500 overseas firms employing 245,000 people directly (IDA Ireland).
- Opening the economy to trade in the late 1950s remains hugely important (Chapter 18).
- Covid-19 showed the economy is heavily dependent on international tourism.
- Covid-19 showed that, due to specialisation, Ireland depends on imports of essential items (e.g. PPE from China); strategically not ideal.
- The Great Depression taught the importance of government spending during a recession to grow the economy.

rows.prompt: What is a positive economic statement?
options: A fact-based statement that can be proved with data
A statement about how things should be
An opinion based on value judgements
A forecast made by the government
rows.explanation: Positive statements are precise and fact-based, so they can be tested with data.

rows.prompt: Which statement is normative?
options: A rise in unemployment results in a fall in incomes
Sales of EVs have risen as carbon taxes rose
The government should raise the minimum wage
The sugar tax reduced demand for sugary drinks
rows.explanation: It says what the government 'should' do, which is a value judgement, not a fact.

rows.prompt: Which statement is positive?
options: The government should abolish USC
When demand for Irish exports rises, employment in exporting firms rises
Milk should cost 3 euro per litre
The government should supply basic health care to all
rows.explanation: This can be checked against data, so it is a positive statement.

rows.prompt: Why will positive statements be especially useful in your research study?
options: The research study is marked on opinions
Normative statements are not allowed in economics
Positive statements are always shorter
The research study must be backed up with data
rows.explanation: The chapter says the research study requires facts and figures, so positive statements are used in particular.

rows.prompt: What percentage of Leaving Cert Economics marks goes to the research study?
rows.explanation: The final exam is worth 80% and the research study 20%.

rows.prompt: What is opportunity cost?
options: The best alternative foregone when a choice is made
The total cost of all the options available
The interest paid on borrowed money
The price paid for a good or service
rows.explanation: When limited resources force a choice, the opportunity cost is the best alternative given up.

rows.prompt: The government has 1 billion euro and chooses Metrolink. In the chapter's example, what does it forego?
options: Nothing, as it can borrow for free
Only the Galway bypass
The corporation tax revenue from MNCs
The motorway, the bypass and 10,000 new homes
rows.explanation: Each project costs 1 billion euro, so choosing Metrolink means the other three projects are given up.

rows.prompt: According to the chapter, what is a risk of raising Ireland's corporation tax from 12.5% to 20%?
options: Unemployment benefits would automatically rise
MNCs might relocate and future revenue could fall
The EU would fine the Irish Government
Property prices would fall sharply

rows.prompt: What is a problem with borrowing to fund all four capital projects?
options: Borrowed money must be repaid with interest by future taxpayers
Borrowing is banned under Irish law
The banks would refuse to lend to the state

rows.explanation: Government debt was forecast near 240 billion euro by 2021 and must be repaid with interest by future taxpayers.

rows.prompt: What date is known as Black Thursday?

23 June 2016
24 October 1929

options: The government set stock prices by law
Widespread speculation pushed prices above actual values
Industrial production had doubled

rows.prompt: Which economist argued for government spending to grow the economy during the Depression?
options: T.K. Whitaker
Franklin D. Roosevelt
Adam Smith
John Maynard Keynes

Ireland's 1958 plan for economic expansion
US public works programmes that created jobs and demand

options: Over 400,000 people emigrated

A shortage of farm workers

rows.prompt: Under EU fiscal rules, a member state's public debt cannot exceed what share of GDP?
rows.explanation: Public debt is limited to 60% of GDP; the current budget deficit is limited to 3%.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a positive and a normative economic statement, giving one example of each.
rows.model_answer: A positive statement is fact-based and can be proved with data, e.g. 'a rise in unemployment results in a fall in incomes'. A normative statement is an opinion about how things should be, based on value judgements, e.g. 'the government should raise the minimum wage to reduce poverty'.

rows.prompt: Using the homelessness example, explain why the solution to an economic problem is not always simple.
rows.model_answer: Building 10,000 homes for 1 billion euro seems obvious, but the government has limited resources and other projects (Metrolink, a motorway, a bypass) compete for the same money. Choosing one means foregoing the others (opportunity cost). Borrowing adds to debt repaid with interest, and raising corporation tax could drive MNCs away.

rows.prompt: Outline the events that led to the Great Depression.
rows.model_answer: The US economy grew in the 1920s and millions invested savings and borrowed money in the stock market, so speculation pushed prices above real values. On Black Thursday, 24 October 1929, nervous investors sold and prices collapsed. Investment fell, unemployment rose, consumer spending fell, and bank runs led to bank failures.

rows.prompt: Name four economic problems facing Ireland in the 1950s.
rows.model_answer: High unemployment; high emigration (over 400,000 emigrated); a falling population (just under 2.9 million in 1956); low incomes and high taxes; overdependence on agriculture; low industrial development.

rows.prompt: Give four reasons why property prices rose during the Celtic Tiger period.
rows.model_answer: FDI increased jobs and incomes; emigration fell and many immigrated, raising demand for homes; low-interest mortgages were easily available; poor regulation meant banks gave excessive loans to people with insecure jobs and lent recklessly to developers.

rows.prompt: What is a bank run and why did the government want to prevent one in 2008?
rows.model_answer: A bank run is when depositors panic, lose confidence and all try to withdraw their savings at once. Banks use deposits to fund lending, so they quickly run out of cash. If Anglo Irish Bank collapsed, panic could spread and cause runs on other banks.

rows.prompt: Why did Ireland seek a bailout from the troika in 2010-2011?
rows.model_answer: Tax revenue fell sharply in the recession while current spending (e.g. social welfare) rose. The government could not borrow normally because Ireland was seen as high-risk. Banks also faced a liquidity crisis as depositors withdrew savings despite the guarantee.

rows.prompt: State three lessons learned from Covid-19 and other events in Ireland's economic history.
rows.model_answer: Covid-19 showed Ireland is heavily dependent on international tourism, and that specialisation left it dependent on imports of essentials like PPE from China. The property crash led the Central Bank to restrict mortgage sizes. The Great Depression showed the importance of government spending in a recession.

rows.prompt: Discuss the economic advantages and disadvantages for Ireland of membership of the European Union. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: Advantages: (1) Free movement of goods and services gives Irish firms access to a market of 448 million people with no tariffs. (2) FDI: foreign firms, e.g. Japanese firms, locate in Ireland to gain free access to the EU market and avoid tariffs. (3) Higher employment due to exports and FDI. (4) Free movement of people lets Irish citizens live, work and study across the EU. (5) The EU negotiates trade deals as a powerful bloc, giving Ireland more bargaining power. Disadvantages: (1) Firms from 26 other states compete freely in Ireland, so Irish firms may lose business and import spending reduces national income. (2) Ireland's EU budget contribution rises with GDP (3.67 billion euro expected in 2021). (3) Loss of control: Ireland cannot pass laws that contradict EU law and can be fined. (4) Fiscal rules limit the current budget deficit to 3% of GDP and debt to 60% of GDP. (5) Ireland cannot make its own trade deals with non-EU countries.
rows.marking_scheme: 5 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation). At least one advantage and one disadvantage required for full marks. Credit any of: access to 448m market, FDI, employment, free movement of people, trading bloc power; import competition, EU budget contribution, loss of control over laws, fiscal rules (3% CBD / 60% debt), no independent trade deals.

rows.prompt: (a) Explain the reasons why the Irish Government sought assistance from the troika in 2010. (b) Outline the economic implications of the bailout for Ireland. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) Government current revenue fell sharply as tax revenue dropped in the recession after the crash. Current spending rose, e.g. higher social welfare costs from rising unemployment, creating large current budget deficits. The government struggled to borrow by selling bonds as Ireland was viewed as high-risk. By late 2010 banks faced a liquidity crisis as depositors withdrew savings despite the Bank Guarantee. (b) Lower standard of living: spending cuts to social welfare and the public sector pay bill, and new taxes such as the USC in 2011. Loss of sovereignty: the IMF and European Commission controlled fiscal policy until December 2013. Interest was charged on the 67.5 billion euro borrowed. The banking sector was restructured into two pillar banks (AIB and Bank of Ireland), with Anglo Irish Bank and Irish Nationwide liquidated.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 2 reasons x 5 marks (2 + 3). (b) 2 implications x 5 marks (2 + 3). Credit: fall in revenue, rise in spending/deficits, inability to borrow, bank liquidity crisis; lower living standards/austerity, loss of sovereignty, interest costs, bank restructuring.

rows.prompt: Outline three implications for the Irish economy of the UK's decision to leave the EU. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: 1. Trade risk: free movement of goods and services between Ireland and the UK was put at risk; without the December 2020 deal, tariffs and quotas would apply. Even with the deal, extra paperwork adds costs and delays at ports, and 2016-2020 brought costly uncertainty and contingency planning. 2. Relocation of firms: some Irish exporters had an incentive to move operations to the UK, while UK firms serving the EU had an incentive to relocate to Ireland, the only remaining English-speaking EU state, e.g. Barclays Bank. 3. Exchange rates: sterling fell sharply after the vote, making Irish exports to the UK more expensive and less competitive.

rows.prompt: Explain how the Great Depression shaped economic thinking and the response of policymakers. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The Great Depression showed that when investment and consumer spending collapse, unemployment rises and a downturn can last for years. Economist John Maynard Keynes argued that government should inject money into the economy through spending to create jobs, raise consumer spending and grow the economy. US President Roosevelt's New Deal applied this by funding public works such as bridges, dams and highways. A lasting lesson is the importance of government spending during a recession.
